summary: This RFC specifies a SASL mechanism and a GSS-API mechanism for SAML 2.0, so existing SAML identity providers can be integrated into non-web applications that use SASL or GSS-API.

eli5.summary: Web sites use one login system and other apps use another. This lets the other apps use the web login system.

questions: what is the saml20 sasl mechanism
how does saml work with imap and xmpp
subtitle: How mail, chat and other non-web apps can log users in through a SAML identity provider, using SASL.

tldr.problem: SAML is widely used for web single sign-on, but applications that authenticate through SASL or GSS-API, such as IMAP and XMPP, had no way to use an existing SAML Identity Provider.
tldr.mechanism: A SASL mechanism named SAML20 carries a domain name to the server, which replies with a URI that sends the user to the Identity Provider. The login itself happens outside SASL, and the server then reports the outcome.
tldr.outcome: Existing SAML Identity Providers can be reused unchanged, with changes needed only in the client and the relying party. The same mechanism also works as a GSS-API mechanism through GS2.

today: RFC 6595 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the SAML20 SASL and GSS-API mechanism, built on RFC 4422 and RFC 5801.

sections.title: Why SAML Meets SASL
sections.content:
SAML 2.0 lets a user be identified to a Relying Party (RP) through signed assertions issued by an Identity Provider (IdP). It is commonly used for Web Single Sign-On. SASL (RFC 4422) is a generic framework for authenticating users in application protocols such as IMAP, POP and XMPP, so that new authentication mechanisms can be plugged in. The GSS-API (RFC 2743) is a similar framework for programs.

This RFC defines a SASL mechanism for SAML and, through the GS2 bridge of RFC 5801, a GSS-API mechanism too. The GSS-API side is optional for SASL implementers.

The design reuses the Web Browser SSO profile of SAML as far as possible. It sets up no separate authentication, integrity or confidentiality layer and assumes a layer such as TLS is in use. It suits clients that have a browser instance available. Browserless SAML profiles, such as the Enhanced Client or Proxy profile, are outside its scope.
sections.eli5: Web sites and other apps use different front doors for logging in. This RFC builds a hallway between them, so an email app can use the web login you already have.

sections.title: The Authentication Flow
sections.content:
In the usual web flow, the browser asks the RP for a resource, the RP redirects it to the IdP, the user logs in there, and the IdP redirects the browser back with an assertion that the user authenticated. The SASL version follows the same shape, with the IdP left untouched. Only the RP (the SASL server) and the client need new code.

  1. The SASL server advertises the SAML20 mechanism.
  2. The client starts SAML20 and sends a domain name that lets the server find the right IdP.
  3. The server sends an authentication request encoded as a URI, which redirects to the IdP for that domain.
  4. The client answers with =. The real answer to the challenge reaches the server out of band.
  5. The client builds a URL from the server's message and hands it to the IdP, directly or through a handler such as a browser.
  6. The user authenticates to the IdP. How is outside SAML and this document, and happens outside SASL.
  7. The IdP tells the SASL server the result as an authentication statement or failure, through the client's browser or handler. This also happens outside SASL.
  8. The SASL server sends the final SASL response to the client.

If the client already holds a valid SAML token, the user need not be involved again, but that is external to SASL.
sections.eli5: The email app asks the mail server to let you in. The server says go and show your ID at the login office. You do, the office tells the server you are who you say, and the server then lets you in.

sections.title: The SAML20 SASL Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism is named SAML20. It can transfer an authorization identity through the gs2-header and offers no security layer of its own. It is client-first, with four mechanism messages: the client's initial-response, the server's authentication-request, the client's fixed message =, and the server's outcome. If the application protocol cannot send a client response with the authentication request, the server sends an empty challenge so the client can begin.

The initial response is the GS2 header followed by an IdP-Identifier, which is a domain name that maps to an IdP. In the GS2 header, gs2-nonstd-flag MUST NOT be present and gs2-cb-flag MUST be n, because channel binding data cannot be integrity protected by the SAML negotiation. The gs2-authzid optionally carries the authorization identity.

The IdP-Identifier is a traditional or an internationalized domain name. Clients and servers MUST treat it as a domain name slot and SHOULD support internationalized names, using A-labels or NR-LDH labels, with U-labels converted by Punycode before sending.

The authentication request is a URI, built per the SAML HTTP Redirect Binding, that carries the SAML request. The client sends it as an HTTP GET over a server-authenticated TLS channel to the IdP. After login, the IdP redirects to the RP's AssertionConsumerServiceURL with the SAML response. The server must act as a SAML RP and match the response to its session using the ID of the request it issued. The SASL server then validates the response, and the result sets its state and is reported to the client as the SASL outcome. How a server maps a domain to an IdP is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The app first says which login office to use. The server hands back a special link to that office. The app answers with a single equals sign, meaning go ahead, and waits to be told whether the login worked.

sections.title: The GSS-API Mechanism
sections.content:
Used through the GS2 bridge, the GSS-API mechanism behaves like the SASL one. The SAML user is the GSS-API Initiator and the RP is the Acceptor. The IdP has no GSS-API role. The messages are the same, except that the GS2 header and channel binding data are left out, and the initial context token header from RFC 2743 is prefixed to the client's first message.

The mechanism OID is 1.3.6.1.5.5.17. Security contexts MUST have GSS_C_MUTUAL_FLAG set to TRUE and, because SAML does not support credential delegation, GSS_C_DELEG_FLAG set to FALSE. Per-message tokens and the GSS_Pseudo_random() function are not supported.

Mutual authentication depends on the application matching the TLS server's identity to the negotiated target name, as described in RFC 6125. The client MUST reject the connection on a mismatch. Initiators use only the name type GSS_C_NT_USER_NAME, and acceptors can use generic types such as GSS_C_NT_HOSTBASED_SERVICE.
sections.eli5: Some programs use a different kind of door that works the same way. This RFC says how the same login trick fits that door, and that the program must double-check it is really talking to the right server.

sections.title: XMPP and IMAP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC walks through a full XMPP login. The server lists DIGEST-MD5, PLAIN and SAML20. The client picks SAML20 and sends a base64 string that decodes to n,,example.org. The server replies with a base64-encoded redirect URL to saml.example.org carrying a SAML authentication request, and the client answers with = (base64 PQ==). The browser steps are shown in brackets as out of scope. The server finishes with success or with a not-authorized failure. If no request can be built, it returns temporary-auth-failure.

The IMAP example does the same after STARTTLS: the server advertises AUTH=SAML20, and the client sends AUTHENTICATE SAML20 and the same initial response.

In both examples the server can use the request ID in the SAML authentication request to correlate the SASL session with the SAML authentication.
sections.eli5: The examples show a chat app and an email app each going through the same steps, with the long scrambled-looking text being the special login link.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanism MUST only be used over channels protected by TLS, or similar integrity-protected and authenticated channels, and the client MUST validate the server's certificate. An intranet does not count as such a channel. Without server identity verification, the mechanism is open to man-in-the-middle and tunneling attacks.

The server is responsible for binding credentials to an authorization identity, so only specific trusted IdPs should be allowed. On privacy, the IdP knows each RP a user logs into, and nothing in the protocol hides this. RPs can also collude by linking data if the same identifier is used everywhere. SAML's targeted identity helps, because the IdP can give each RP its own opaque identifier. For GSS-API use, proper TLS server identity verification is critical.
sections.eli5: Only use this on a locked, checked connection, and only trust login offices you picked. The login office can see which places you visit, so privacy tools matter.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered the SASL mechanism profile SAML20 with intended usage COMMON, owned by the IETF. It also assigned a new entry in the SMI Security for Mechanism Codes sub-registry, under the prefix 1.3.6.1.5.5, for the GSS mechanism.
sections.eli5: The official lists of login methods got a new line for this one, so nobody else uses the same name or number.

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
initial-response = gs2-header IdP-Identifier
IdP-Identifier = domain ; domain name with corresponding IdP

authentication-request = URI
